events.intro: Star Wars Day falls on May 4 every year, the date fans across the galaxy celebrate with the pun 'May the Fourth be with you.' This countdown is to Star Wars Day {YEAR}, ticking down live to May 4.

sections.p: The date is a play on the saga's most famous line, 'May the Force be with you.' Fans had been making the pun for years, and it has since grown into a worldwide celebration officially embraced by Lucasfilm and Disney.
Expect movie marathons, themed merchandise drops, special events at Disney parks, and a wave of posts online. The unofficial 'Revenge of the Fifth' follows the next day, May 5.

timeline.text: The earliest documented use of the pun appeared in Britain: London's Evening News reportedly ran a message congratulating incoming prime minister Margaret Thatcher with 'May the Fourth Be With You, Maggie.'
Fan Albin Johnson founded the 501st Legion, a stormtrooper costuming club that grew into a worldwide organization and became one of the pun's most visible costumed ambassadors.

After roughly 200 501st Legion members marched in the Tournament of Roses Parade with George Lucas as grand marshal, the group entered the Guinness World Records book as the largest Star Wars costuming group.
Toronto comedians staged what's considered the first organized public Star Wars Day event, featuring trivia, a costume contest, and a 35mm screening of the original film.

Following its 2012 acquisition of Lucasfilm, Disney began officially marking May the Fourth with Star Wars Day festivities at Disneyland and Walt Disney World, a tradition the parks have expanded every year since.
The Kalamazoo Wings minor-league hockey team set a Guinness World Record for the largest lightsaber battle, with 3,889 fans dueling for nearly four minutes during a Star Wars Night game.

events.name: George Washington's Birthday
events.title: Washington's Birthday Countdown: February 22
events.desc: Live countdown to George Washington's birthday on February 22, the history of the holiday, Presidents' Day, and why America still celebrates it.
events.intro: George Washington, the first President of the United States, was born on February 22, 1732, in Westmoreland County, Virginia. His birthday became one of America's first federal holidays, this countdown runs to the {NTH} anniversary of his birth on {DATE}.

sections.p: Americans celebrated Washington's birthday during his own lifetime, and Congress made it a federal holiday in 1879, the first to honor an individual. The federal observance falls on the third Monday of February, which is why many people know it as Presidents' Day, but the actual birthday is February 22.

Washington was actually born on February 11, 1731, under the old Julian calendar. When Britain and its colonies switched to the Gregorian calendar in 1752, his birthday moved to February 22, 1732, so he aged a year and 11 days on paper overnight.

facts: Born February 22, 1732, in Westmoreland County, Virginia
Commander-in-chief of the Continental Army, president 1789, 1797
His birthday became a federal holiday in 1879
Mount Vernon holds celebrations on the actual date every year

sections.h: The president who preserved the Union
sections.p: Lincoln led the country through the Civil War, issued the Emancipation Proclamation, and delivered the Gettysburg Address, 272 words that redefined the nation. His birthday was widely observed within years of his death in 1865.

Lincoln's Birthday is a legal holiday or observance in states including Illinois, the Land of Lincoln, as well as Connecticut, Missouri and New York. Nationally, he's honored together with Washington around Presidents' Day each February.

facts: Born February 12, 1809, near Hodgenville, Kentucky

The Gettysburg Address is just 272 words long

events.title: Christmas {YEAR} Countdown: How Many Days Until Christmas?
events.desc: Live Christmas countdown to December 25, days, hours, minutes and seconds. The history of Christmas, how it's celebrated worldwide, and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: Christmas falls on December 25 every year, celebrating the birth of Jesus and, for billions of people, family, generosity and light in the middle of winter. This countdown is to Christmas {YEAR}, ticking down to the morning of December 25, live.

sections.p: The first recorded December 25 celebration of Christ's birth dates to Rome in 336 AD. Over the centuries it absorbed midwinter traditions, evergreens, feasting, gift-giving, and grew into both a major Christian feast and a global cultural holiday.

Gifts arrive from Santa Claus, Père Noël, or the Christkind depending on where you are; some countries open presents on Christmas Eve, others on the morning of the 25th. In Japan, fried chicken became a Christmas tradition; in Australia, it's celebrated in midsummer on the beach.

facts: First recorded December 25 celebration: Rome, 336 AD
A federal holiday in the United States since 1870
“Jingle Bells” was originally written for Thanksgiving
Japan's KFC Christmas tradition dates to 1974

timeline.text: Puritan leaders in the Massachusetts Bay Colony banned public Christmas celebrations outright, fining anyone caught feasting or skipping work for the holiday five shillings; the law stood for 22 years before being repealed.

London civil servant Henry Cole commissioned the first commercial Christmas card the same year Charles Dickens published 'A Christmas Carol,' together reviving Victorian interest in charity, feasting, and family gathering as holiday hallmarks.

The Illustrated London News published an engraving of Queen Victoria, Prince Albert, and their children around a decorated tree at Windsor Castle, spreading the German royal custom of the Christmas tree through Britain and America.
Edward H. Johnson, a business associate of Thomas Edison, hand-wired 80 red, white, and blue bulbs onto a rotating tree at his New York home, creating the first electrically lit Christmas tree.

President Calvin Coolidge pressed a button to light the first National Christmas Tree, a 48-foot Vermont balsam fir strung with 2,500 bulbs on the White House Ellipse, launching an annual presidential tradition.

Coca-Cola commissioned illustrator Haddon Sundblom to paint a warm, rosy-cheeked Santa Claus for its magazine ads, cementing the now-standard jolly image of Santa across more than three decades of campaigns.
Bing Crosby recorded Irving Berlin's 'White Christmas' in just 18 minutes; it went on to sell an estimated 50 million copies, making it the best-selling single of all time.

events.desc: Live Halloween countdown to October 31, the Celtic origins of the holiday, trick-or-treating history, and a shareable spooky countdown.
events.intro: Halloween lands on October 31 every year, a night of costumes, candy and jack-o'-lanterns with roots more than two thousand years old. This countdown is to Halloween {YEAR}, ticking down to October 31, live.

sections.p: Halloween traces back to Samhain, the Celtic festival marking summer's end, when the boundary between worlds was said to thin. Christianity layered All Hallows' Eve on top of it, Irish and Scottish immigrants carried the customs to North America, and trick-or-treating took its modern form in the 1930s, 50s.
The carved pumpkin comes from the Irish legend of Stingy Jack, doomed to wander with a burning coal in a hollow turnip. In America, the native pumpkin proved much easier to carve, and much bigger.

facts: Rooted in Samhain, a Celtic harvest festival over 2,000 years old
Second-largest commercial holiday in the United States
Jack-o'-lanterns were originally carved from turnips
Trick-or-treating became widespread in the 1950s

timeline.text: Waves of Irish and Scottish immigrants, many fleeing the Great Famine, carried Halloween customs to the United States, turning a regional folk tradition into a nationally celebrated holiday by the late 19th century.
The phrase 'trick or treat' appeared in print for the first time, as costumed children going door-to-door for treats spread across American and Canadian towns.
A wave of Halloween vandalism grew so severe it was dubbed 'Black Halloween,' pushing communities to organize supervised parties, parades, and trick-or-treat rounds to redirect the mischief.
In Philadelphia, a Presbyterian minister's family launched the first Trick-or-Treat for UNICEF collection, turning door-to-door candy runs into a fundraiser for children overseas.
Charity groups such as the Jaycees began staging haunted-house fundraisers nationwide, spawning the commercial haunted-attraction industry that now spans thousands of venues each fall.

Puppeteer Ralph Lee led an informal procession of masks and puppets through Greenwich Village, the seed of what grew into New York's Village Halloween Parade, now billed as the world's largest Halloween parade.
US Halloween spending hit a record $13.1 billion, according to the National Retail Federation, topping the previous high of $12.2 billion set in 2023.

events.desc: Live countdown to Valentine's Day on February 14, the story of St. Valentine, how the day became about love, and a romantic countdown to share.
events.intro: Valentine's Day arrives every February 14, the world's holiday of love, from handwritten cards to candlelit dinners. This countdown is to Valentine's Day {YEAR}, ticking down live to February 14.

sections.p: The day is named for a third-century Roman martyr, by legend, a priest who performed forbidden weddings for soldiers. The romantic association came a thousand years later, when Chaucer and the poets of courtly love linked mid-February to pairing birds and lovers' notes.

Roughly 145 million Valentine's cards are exchanged in the US alone each year, and that's not counting classroom valentines. Japan flips the tradition: women give chocolate on February 14, and men reciprocate on White Day, March 14.

facts: Named for a 3rd-century Roman martyr, St. Valentine
Linked to romance by Chaucer in the 14th century
About 145 million cards are exchanged in the US each year

timeline.text: Rome's Lupercalia fertility festival, held each February 13-15 with animal sacrifice and ritual matchmaking, is first traced to this era. Most historians now doubt it directly inspired Valentine's Day.
Pope Gelasius I formally forbids Christians from taking part in the pagan Lupercalia festival.
Pope Gelasius I declares February 14 a feast day honoring the martyr St. Valentine, though scholars still debate whether this was meant to replace Lupercalia.

Massachusetts entrepreneur Esther Howland creates elaborate lace-and-flower valentine prototypes and, the following year, builds an assembly-line workshop that turns valentine-making into American big business.
The New England Confectionery Company (Necco) begins printing short phrases onto candy 'Mottoes,' the direct ancestor of the heart-shaped Sweethearts conversation candy.

Thirteen American florists meeting in Rochester, New York found Florists' Telegraph Delivery (FTD), the first flowers-by-wire network, letting customers send fresh flowers to distant cities the same day.
Hallmark, which had sold Valentine's postcards since 1910, adds boxed valentine greeting cards to its lineup, helping cement the mass-market card industry.

events.desc: Live countdown to Thanksgiving (the fourth Thursday of November), the history from Plymouth to the Macy's parade, and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: Thanksgiving falls on the fourth Thursday of November in the United States, a feast built around gratitude, family and a very large turkey. This countdown is to Thanksgiving {YEAR} on {DATE}, updating automatically each year.

sections.h: From Plymouth to a national holiday
sections.p: The 1621 harvest feast shared by the Plymouth colonists and the Wampanoag is the traditional origin story. Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for decades to make it national, and Abraham Lincoln proclaimed it a nationwide holiday in 1863, in the middle of the Civil War.

The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade has marched since 1924, the presidential turkey pardon became an annual ritual, and football and Black Friday shopping now bracket the meal. Canada celebrates its own Thanksgiving on the second Monday of October.

facts: Made a national holiday by Lincoln in 1863
Fixed to the fourth Thursday of November in 1941
The Macy's parade has run since 1924
About 46 million turkeys are eaten each Thanksgiving

timeline.text: English colonists at Plymouth and roughly 90 Wampanoag led by the sachem Massasoit (Ousamequin) shared a three-day autumn harvest gathering — the event now remembered as the 'First Thanksgiving,' though no one called it that at the time.

Magazine editor Sarah Josepha Hale campaigned for decades — first in her 1827 novel Northwood, then annually in Godey's Lady's Book — petitioning governors and five successive presidents to establish one fixed national Thanksgiving date.

To extend the Christmas shopping season during the Depression, FDR moved Thanksgiving a week earlier to November's next-to-last Thursday. The switch, mocked as 'Franksgiving,' left 22 states on the new date, 23 on the old one, and three observing both.

After two years of a split holiday, Congress passed a joint resolution — signed into law by Roosevelt on December 26, 1941 — permanently fixing Thanksgiving as the fourth Thursday in November nationwide.

The National Turkey Federation presented President Truman with the first 'National Thanksgiving Turkey,' starting an annual White House photo tradition, though Truman himself is not documented as having spared any bird.

After Thanksgiving turkey sales left Swanson with 260 tons of unsold birds, salesman Gerry Thomas helped devise the three-compartment frozen tray that became the Swanson TV Dinner, launching the frozen-meal industry.

President George H.W. Bush was the first to formally declare a turkey 'pardoned,' sending it to live out its days on a farm — turning earlier informal gestures by JFK and Reagan into the annual tradition still practiced today.

events.desc: Live countdown to midnight on New Year's Eve, the history of January 1, the Times Square ball drop, and a shareable countdown to the new year.
events.intro: The new year begins at midnight on January 1, and this countdown ticks to your local midnight to ring in {YEAR}, wherever you are. Fireworks in Sydney, the ball drop in Times Square, grapes in Madrid: one moment, celebrated around the planet for 24 straight hours.

sections.p: January is named for Janus, the Roman god of beginnings who looks both backward and forward. Julius Caesar fixed January 1 as the year's start in 45 BC, and the Gregorian calendar carried it worldwide.

The Times Square ball has dropped since 1907 (originally made of iron and wood with 100 light bulbs). Spaniards eat twelve grapes at the twelve strokes of midnight; Danes smash plates on friends' doorsteps; Japan rings temple bells 108 times.

The Times Square ball first dropped in 1907
Sydney's fireworks reach a global TV audience of over a billion
“Auld Lang Syne” is a Robert Burns poem from 1788

timeline.text: Pope Gregory XIII's papal bull Inter gravissimas established the Gregorian calendar, correcting the Julian calendar's leap-year drift; Catholic countries adopted it within months, cementing January 1 as New Year's Day across most of Europe.
Times Square's original iron-and-wood ball was retired after over a decade of use and replaced with a 400-pound ball made entirely of wrought iron.
The iron ball gave way to a much lighter aluminum version weighing just 150 pounds, the design that would drop for the next four decades.
Dick Clark's New Year's Rockin' Eve premiered on NBC on December 31, 1972, with Clark reporting live from Times Square; it later moved to ABC and became the top-rated US New Year's special.
For the millennium, Times Square unveiled an entirely new ball covered in 504 Waterford Crystal panels, replacing the old aluminum ball's halogen bulbs for a global Y2K audience.
Marking the ball drop's 100th anniversary, a fifth redesign switched to LED technology, with 672 crystal panels lit by 9,576 Philips LEDs capable of millions of colors.

events.desc: Live countdown to the Fourth of July, the story of the Declaration of Independence, fireworks traditions, and a shareable Independence Day countdown.
events.h1: Countdown to the Fourth of July
events.intro: Independence Day commemorates July 4, 1776, when the Continental Congress adopted the Declaration of Independence. Fireworks, parades and cookouts have marked the date ever since, this countdown is to July 4th, {YEAR}, ticking down live.

sections.p: Independence was actually voted on July 2; the Declaration's final text was adopted July 4, which became the date on the document and in the national memory. John Adams predicted celebrations with 'pomp and parade… bonfires and illuminations', he just expected them two days earlier.
Thomas Jefferson and John Adams, the Declaration's author and its fiercest advocate, both died on July 4, 1826, exactly fifty years after its adoption. James Monroe died on July 4 five years later.

facts: The Declaration was adopted July 4, 1776
Most signers actually signed on August 2, 1776
Jefferson and Adams both died on July 4, 1826
Americans set off some 280 million pounds of fireworks each year

timeline.text: Philadelphia marks the first anniversary of independence with a 13-gun salute from ships on the Delaware, a Congressional dinner, bell-ringing, and a fireworks display over the Commons — even though Congress itself nearly let the day pass unmarked.
Congress makes July 4th a national holiday, but only for federal workers in Washington, D.C., and unpaid.
Nearly seven decades later, Congress finally makes July 4th a paid holiday for all federal employees, grouping it with Christmas, Thanksgiving, Labor Day, and other now-familiar federal holidays.

The Bicentennial brings Operation Sail's 200-plus tall ships up New York Harbor before roughly six million spectators, the same year Macy's launches the fireworks show that grows into the nation's largest annual Independence Day display.

As states loosen fireworks laws, the US consumer fireworks industry balloons from about $407 million in annual revenue to roughly $2.3 billion, turning backyard pyrotechnics into a multibillion-dollar seasonal business.

The nation marks its Semiquincentennial — 250 years since the Declaration — with a Washington, D.C. fireworks show of 850,000 shells launched from 10 sites over 40 minutes, breaking the world record for the largest fireworks display in history.

events.label: Summer Solstice
events.name: Summer Solstice
events.title: Summer Solstice Countdown: The Longest Day of the Year
events.desc: Live countdown to the summer solstice around June 20, 21, why it's the longest day, Stonehenge and midsummer traditions, and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: The summer solstice, around June 20, 21 in the Northern Hemisphere, is the longest day of the year, when Earth's tilt leans your half of the planet closest to the sun. This countdown is to the summer solstice {YEAR} on {DATE}, ticking down live.

sections.p: The solstice is a precise astronomical moment: the sun reaches its northernmost point in the sky. Above the Arctic Circle it doesn't set at all, the midnight sun, while the Southern Hemisphere marks its shortest day.

Thousands gather at Stonehenge, whose stones align with the solstice sunrise. Sweden's Midsummer is practically a national holiday of maypoles and flower crowns, and bonfires burn across northern Europe, traditions older than written history.

facts: Falls on June 20, 21 or 22 depending on the year
Stonehenge aligns with the solstice sunrise
Above the Arctic Circle the sun never sets that day
“Solstice” means “sun stands still” in Latin

timeline.text: Stonehenge's massive sarsen stones were erected and precisely positioned so the monument's central axis frames the sun rising over the Heel Stone on the summer solstice.

Public solstice gatherings at Stonehenge trace to the opening of the railway to Salisbury, which made the site newly accessible; by the turn of the 20th century, Druid revivalists began holding their own solstice ceremonies there.

Scandinavians have marked the summer solstice since the Iron Age with bonfires, dancing and fertility rituals intended to honor the sun and secure a good harvest, well predating any Christian calendar.

As Christianity spread through Scandinavia, the Church folded the older solstice rites into the feast of St John the Baptist on June 24, and the flower-garlanded maypole became a central part of the Midsummer festivities.

Sweden moved Midsummer's Eve off its fixed June 24 date to the nearest Friday so the holiday would reliably fall on a long weekend; it functions as a de facto national public holiday alongside Christmas.
Seattle's Fremont Solstice Parade was founded, growing into a signature modern solstice festival.

events.intro: St. Patrick's Day falls on March 17 every year, a celebration of Ireland's patron saint that has grown into a worldwide festival of all things green. This countdown is to St. Patrick's Day {YEAR}, ticking down live to March 17.

sections.p: Patrick wasn't actually Irish, he was born in Roman Britain, kidnapped to Ireland as a teenager, and returned later as a missionary. March 17 marks the traditional date of his death around 461 AD, and the shamrock legend comes from his teaching.

New York has held a St. Patrick's Day parade since 1762, Chicago dyes its river green, and cities from Dublin to Tokyo throw festivals. In Ireland it's both a national holiday and, historically, a religious feast day.

timeline.text: Irish Christians begin observing an annual feast day in honor of St. Patrick, the origin of the holiday as a religious commemoration rather than a national celebration.
St. Patrick's feast day is formally added to the Catholic Church's liturgical calendar, largely through the influence of Waterford-born Franciscan scholar Luke Wadding, cementing March 17 churchwide.

During the United Irishmen Rebellion, green — worn on lapels and carried on flags as a symbol of Irish nationalism — begins displacing the lighter 'St. Patrick's blue' that had been the saint's traditional color.

The Great Famine drives more than 1.5 million Irish immigrants to American shores; by 1850 Irish-born residents make up roughly 43% of the country's foreign-born population, and their numbers transform small local observances into major public celebrations.
Rival New York Irish aid societies unite their separate St. Patrick's Day processions into a single official parade, which quickly grows into the largest parade in the United States.
The Bank Holiday (Ireland) Act 1903, introduced by Irish MP James O'Mara, makes St. Patrick's Day an official public holiday in Ireland.

Tourism Ireland launches 'Global Greening' by lighting the Sydney Opera House emerald green on March 17; the initiative later spreads to hundreds of landmarks worldwide, from the Empire State Building to Niagara Falls.

events.desc: Live countdown to Cinco de Mayo on May 5, the real story of the Battle of Puebla and how the day is celebrated.
events.intro: Cinco de Mayo, May 5, commemorates Mexico's victory at the Battle of Puebla in 1862, and despite the common mix-up, it is not Mexico's Independence Day (that's September 16). This countdown is to Cinco de Mayo {YEAR}, ticking down live to May 5.

sections.p: On May 5, 1862, General Ignacio Zaragoza's outnumbered Mexican forces defeated an invading French army at Puebla. The victory became a lasting symbol of Mexican resistance and pride.

sections.h: A bigger party north of the border
sections.p: In Mexico the day is mainly observed in the state of Puebla; in the United States it grew into a broad celebration of Mexican-American culture, food and music.

The first big Cinco de Mayo celebrations happened not in Mexico but in the American West: Mexican communities in California, Nevada, Oregon and Texas began marking the victory in the 1860s, within a year of the battle itself. A century later, Chicano activists of the 1960s revived the date as a symbol of pride, identifying with Mexico's stand against a European invader, and by the 1980s it had grown into the coast-to-coast fiesta Americans know today — helped along by a great deal of advertising.

In Puebla the day means a grand civic parade, and Mexico City's Peñón de los Baños neighborhood stages a full costumed reenactment of the battle every May 5. At home, cook the region's true signature dish: mole poblano, the rich chile-and-chocolate sauce born in Puebla's convents, served over chicken or turkey. Pour the agua fresca, put on some mariachi, and raise a glass to General Zaragoza — that beats a novelty sombrero every time.

timeline.text: Mexican American communities hold the first Cinco de Mayo commemorations in Los Angeles and San Francisco, organized through Juntas Patrióticas Mejicanas that raised money for Mexico's resistance to the French occupation.

California communities keep the commemoration going every year, with more than a hundred Juntas Patrióticas chapters active statewide at their peak; through the early 20th century the day remains largely a local Mexican American tradition.
President Franklin Roosevelt's Good Neighbor Policy toward Latin America helps push Cinco de Mayo toward wider recognition in the US over the following decades.

Chicano civil rights activists on Southwest college campuses adopt the Battle of Puebla and May 5 as a day to publicly assert Mexican American pride, folding the holiday into the broader Chicano Movement.
Anheuser-Busch, Miller and Coors build dedicated Hispanic-marketing divisions and pour tens of millions of dollars into Cinco de Mayo promotions aimed at Latino audiences.
Fiesta Broadway launches in downtown Los Angeles, drawing 50,000 people its first year and growing into what organizers call the largest Cinco de Mayo celebration in the Americas.

sections.p: Anna Jarvis held the first Mother's Day service in Grafton, West Virginia, in 1908 to honor her own mother, and campaigned until President Wilson made it a national observance in 1914.
Jarvis later spent decades fighting the holiday's commercialization, she wanted handwritten letters, not printed cards. The flowers won, but the sentiment endures.

sections.h: The founder who tried to cancel it
sections.p: Anna Jarvis created Mother's Day in 1908 to honor her own mother, and President Wilson made it national in 1914. Then florists and card companies moved in — and Jarvis spent the rest of her life, and most of her inheritance, campaigning to abolish the holiday she'd founded, organizing boycotts and crashing conventions. She died in 1948, penniless, still fighting it.

Jarvis is arrested for disturbing the peace after crashing a Philadelphia carnation-selling convention, part of her escalating campaign against the holiday's commercialization.
Her fortune spent on decades of lawsuits and lobbying, Jarvis is placed in a Pennsylvania sanitarium; unbeknownst to her, florists and greeting-card companies quietly cover her bills.

The holiday spreads worldwide but never settles on one date: the UK keeps Mothering Sunday in Lent, Norway observes it in February, most Arab countries mark it on March 21, and Thailand ties it to the queen's birthday on August 12.

sections.p: Sonora Smart Dodd, raised with her five siblings by a Civil War veteran single father, organized the first Father's Day in Spokane, Washington, in 1910 after hearing a Mother's Day sermon.
It took six decades of on-and-off observance before President Nixon signed Father's Day into permanent law in 1972.

Father's Day exists because Sonora Smart Dodd of Spokane, Washington heard a 1909 Mother's Day sermon and asked a simple question: what about fathers? Hers — Civil War veteran William Jackson Smart — had raised six children alone. The first celebration was held in Spokane in June 1910, but Congress resisted for decades; it only became a permanent national holiday in 1972.

President Woodrow Wilson traveled to Spokane to speak at a Father's Day event, then pressed a telegraph button in Washington, D.C., to unfurl a flag there — informal presidential support, but Congress resisted a formal proclamation.

President Calvin Coolidge recommended that state governments observe Father's Day, urging fathers toward 'the full measure of their obligations,' though he too stopped short of a national proclamation.

Men's clothing retailers, organized as the National Council for the Promotion of Father's Day, began coordinating clothiers, tobacconists, florists, and stationers nationwide behind the slogan 'Give Dad Something to Wear.'

President Lyndon B. Johnson issued the first presidential proclamation for Father's Day on June 15, 1966, formally designating the third Sunday in June and calling for flags to fly on government buildings.

events.intro: Memorial Day falls on the last Monday of May, honoring the American service members who died in the nation's wars. This countdown automatically targets the next one.

sections.p: The observance grew out of Decoration Day, proclaimed in 1868 after the Civil War, when communities decorated soldiers' graves with flowers. It became Memorial Day and moved to the last Monday of May in 1971.
Flags fly at half-staff until noon, Arlington National Cemetery holds its annual ceremony, and at 3 p.m. local time Americans pause for the National Moment of Remembrance.

The red poppies pinned on lapels each May trace to 'In Flanders Fields,' the 1915 poem written after the Second Battle of Ypres. Inspired by it, American professor Moina Michael vowed in 1918 to wear a red poppy year-round in remembrance — and campaigned until veterans' groups adopted it as the official flower of remembrance.

timeline.text: Waterloo, New York, holds a community-wide observance on May 5 — businesses close and residents decorate soldiers' graves — though at least two dozen towns have separately claimed to have started the tradition.

Union veterans' leader General John A. Logan issues General Order No. 11, designating May 30 as 'Decoration Day' for decorating the graves of Civil War dead; the first national observance follows that day at Arlington National Cemetery.
After World War I, the holiday's meaning broadens from honoring only Civil War dead to commemorating American service members lost in any war.

Congress and President Lyndon B. Johnson officially proclaim Waterloo, New York the 'birthplace' of Memorial Day, 100 years after its first observance there — though the claim remains disputed by historians and rival towns.
Federal law formally adopts 'Memorial Day' as the holiday's legal name, cementing a shift in usage from 'Decoration Day' that had been underway for decades.
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act takes effect, making Memorial Day a federal holiday permanently observed on the last Monday of May.
President Bill Clinton signs the National Moment of Remembrance Act, establishing a national pause at 3 p.m. local time on Memorial Day.

events.intro: Labor Day falls on the first Monday of September, honoring American workers and the labor movement. This countdown automatically targets the next one.

sections.p: The first Labor Day parade marched through New York City in 1882, organized by the labor unions. Congress made it a federal holiday in 1894.
Today Labor Day doubles as the unofficial end of summer, the last long weekend before school routines and football season take over.

sections.h: A holiday born of a crisis
sections.p: The federal holiday was signed in the shadow of the 1894 Pullman strike, when a railroad boycott paralyzed the country and federal troops were sent in. Days after the strike collapsed, President Cleveland signed Labor Day into law — a national gesture of reconciliation with American workers, rushed through Congress unanimously.

timeline.text: Carpenters' union leader Peter McGuire is traditionally credited with pitching the idea of a workers' holiday to New York's Central Labor Union, but historians have since found evidence that machinist Matthew Maguire, the union's secretary, was the true organizer.
An estimated 10,000 to 20,000 workers marched from City Hall past a reviewing stand at Union Square to a park uptown, then capped the day with a picnic.
Oregon became the first state to put Labor Day into law, on February 21, 1887; Colorado, Massachusetts, New Jersey, and New York followed later that same year.
By the time Congress acted, roughly 23 states had already established their own Labor Day holidays independently, making federal recognition more a formal catch-up than a new idea.
The 'no white after Labor Day' rule emerged among New York's Gilded Age elite as a class marker, using seasonal wardrobe switches to signal insider status.
US union membership fell to a record-low 9.9% of workers, continuing a decline from about 20% in 1983 — a striking contrast to the labor movement's strength when the holiday was created.

sections.p: Campaigns for a King holiday began days after his assassination in 1968; President Reagan signed it into law in 1983 and it was first observed in 1986. By 2000, all fifty states recognized it.

sections.h: A day on, not a day off
sections.p: MLK Day is the only federal holiday designated as a national day of service, with volunteer projects across the country honoring Dr. King's legacy.

The final push for the holiday came with a melody: Stevie Wonder released 'Happy Birthday' in 1980 as a campaign anthem for a King holiday, toured behind it, and helped deliver a petition of six million signatures to Congress — described as the largest petition in favor of an issue in U.S. history at the time.

Arizona Gov. Bruce Babbitt creates a paid state holiday by executive order after a state bill fails — the opening move in a bitter, years-long holdout.
Arizona voters narrowly reject two competing ballot measures to establish the holiday, leaving the state as a national holdout.

Arizona voters approve the holiday with 62% support in a new referendum; the state goes on to host Super Bowl XXX in Tempe in 1996.
Congress passes the King Holiday and Service Act, signed by President Clinton, formally charging a federal agency with organizing the day as a national day of service.

sections.p: The federal holiday is still legally named Washington's Birthday; the Uniform Monday Holiday Act of 1968 moved it to the third Monday of February, and the broader 'Presidents' Day' name caught on from there.
Because the third Monday can only land between February 15 and 21, the holiday never actually falls on Washington's real birthday, February 22.

sections.p: Federal law still calls this day Washington's Birthday — 'Presidents Day' is a nickname that stuck, boosted by 1970s advertising. Better yet: because the third Monday of February can only land on the 15th through the 21st, the holiday can never actually fall on Washington's real birthday, February 22.

timeline.text: Congress made Washington's Birthday a federal holiday, signed into law by President Rutherford B. Hayes — the first US federal holiday created to honor an individual American's birth.
The holiday initially covered only federal workers in Washington, D.C.; it was extended to federal employees nationwide in 1885, fixed each year on Washington's actual birth date, February 22.

The Uniform Monday Holiday Act passed Congress, part of a push to shift several federal holidays to Mondays and create more three-day weekends. An early draft would have renamed the holiday 'Presidents' Day' and folded in Lincoln's birthday, but the proposal stalled and was dropped before passage.
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act took effect, moving the observance off February 22 for good and onto the third Monday in February.
Retailers began branding February sales as 'Presidents' Day' promotions, and the name caught on with the public even though Congress never wrote it into law.

States still diverge on what to call it: Virginia, Illinois, Iowa, Florida, and New York officially retain 'Washington's Birthday,' while several states separately observe Lincoln's Birthday on February 12.

events.intro: The 2030 FIFA World Cup opens on June 8, 2030 at Estadio Centenario in Montevideo, Uruguay — the ground that staged the very first World Cup final in 1930 — before the tournament moves to its main hosts, Morocco, Portugal and Spain.

sections.p: The centenary edition is split like no World Cup before it. Uruguay, Argentina and Paraguay each stage one opening-round match on June 8 and 9, honouring the tournament's South American birthplace. The rest of the competition is played in Morocco, Portugal and Spain, starting June 13 and 14, and runs through July 21.

Spain arrive at 2030 as holders. They beat Argentina 1-0 after extra time at MetLife Stadium on July 19, 2026, Ferran Torres scoring in the 106th minute for Spain's second world title after 2010. The other two semi-finalists produced a ten-goal bronze final in Miami: England beat France 6-4, with a Bukayo Saka hat-trick. The 2026 edition was the first with 48 teams and 104 matches, played across the United States, Canada and Mexico.

sections.h: One hundred years of the World Cup
sections.p: The first World Cup kicked off in Uruguay in July 1930, with thirteen teams and a purpose-built stadium — the Estadio Centenario — finished only days before the opening matches. Uruguay beat Argentina 4-2 in the final in front of a reported 68,000 people. The 2030 tournament returns to that stadium exactly a century later.

sections.h: The dog who saved the World Cup
sections.p: Four months before England hosted the 1966 tournament, the Jules Rimet trophy was stolen from a London exhibition. A week later a mongrel named Pickles, out for a walk, sniffed it out of a hedge wrapped in newspaper. Pickles became a national hero and got a year's supply of dog food; the thief got two years. Brazil, for the record, remains the only nation to have played in every World Cup.

events.intro: The Games of the XXXIV Olympiad open in Los Angeles on July 14, 2028, the third time LA has hosted, after 1932 and 1984. This countdown runs to the opening ceremony.

sections.p: Los Angeles joins London and Paris as the only cities to host the Summer Games three times. The 1984 LA Games famously turned a profit and reshaped how the Olympics are organized.
The most recent Games were Milano Cortina 2026, where Norway topped the medal table with a record 18 golds. Recent host cities and medal-table leaders are listed below.
LA28 brings new and returning sports, including cricket, flag football, squash and lacrosse, staged across landmarks from the Coliseum, which hosted in both 1932 and 1984, to SoFi Stadium.

sections.h: 1932: the Depression Games that invented the podium
sections.p: LA's first Olympics opened in 1932 with the world mired in the Great Depression — barely half as many athletes made the trip as in 1928. Yet those Games changed the Olympics forever: organizers built the first Olympic Village, 550 bungalows on 321 acres in Baldwin Hills, and gave the brand-new victory podium — first used months earlier at the Lake Placid Winter Games — its modern form, with numbered steps, flag-raising and the winner's national anthem. Against all odds, the 1932 Games still turned a profit of about $1 million — a trick LA famously repeated in 1984.

sections.h: What's at stake in a midterm
sections.p: All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats (33 regular races plus two special elections) are contested, along with 36 governorships and thousands of state and local offices. Midterms regularly reshape the balance of power in Washington.

An 1845 law set federal elections on 'the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November', late enough for the harvest, early enough to beat winter, and on a day that let rural voters travel after Sunday church without conflicting with market Wednesdays.

Midterm results have repeatedly reshaped Washington: 1994's “Republican Revolution” flipped 54 House seats and delivered the GOP its first House majority in 40 years; 2006 handed Democrats both chambers amid war-weariness; and 2010's “shellacking” swung 63 House seats to Republicans, the largest one-election shift since 1948. Midterms are also historically a referendum on the sitting president — turnout and the national mood in the months before Election Day tend to matter more than any single local race.

sections.p: Diwali celebrates the victory of light over darkness and good over evil. Homes and streets glow with rows of oil lamps (diyas), candles and fireworks, and families gather to share sweets and exchange gifts.
Observed by over a billion people, Diwali is a public holiday across India and in many other countries, and is marked by Hindu, Jain, Sikh and Buddhist communities worldwide.

sections.h: Rama's homecoming, retold in 2.6 million lamps
sections.p: The most beloved Diwali story tells of Prince Rama returning to Ayodhya after 14 years of exile and victory over the demon king Ravana; the city's people lit rows of clay lamps to guide him home. Modern Ayodhya restages that welcome on an astonishing scale: at Deepotsav 2025, volunteers lit 2,617,215 oil lamps along the Saryu River — a Guinness World Record verified by drone count — while 2,128 people performed aarti together, setting a second record the same night.

sections.h: Five nights to try at home
sections.p: Diwali is really a five-day arc. It opens with Dhanteras, when homes are cleaned top to bottom and families buy something metal for luck. Choti Diwali follows with an early oil-bath ritual. The main night belongs to Lakshmi Puja: lay a rangoli of colored powder or flower petals at the door, light clay diyas in windows and share mithai (sweets). Govardhan Puja brings mountains of festive food, and Bhai Dooj closes the festival honoring the bond between siblings.

sections.p: The most important holiday in much of East and Southeast Asia, it ushers in a new year of the 12-animal zodiac with family reunions, red envelopes, lion dances, fireworks and feasts. Celebrations traditionally run for about fifteen days.
Each year is associated with one of twelve zodiac animals. The festival is celebrated by well over a billion people across China, Korea, Vietnam and diaspora communities worldwide.

sections.h: The beast that made the holiday loud and red
sections.p: Legend says the traditions began with Nian, a monster that crept out of the mountains every New Year's Eve to raid villages — until people discovered it feared three things: the color red, bright firelight and loud noise. Ever since, doors get dressed in red paper couplets, lanterns burn through the night and firecrackers rattle the streets to chase the old year's bad luck away. The legend still shapes the holiday's real-world footprint too: China's chunyun travel rush around the festival spans about 40 days, the largest annual human migration on Earth.

The heart of the holiday is New Year's Eve: families clean the house beforehand to sweep out old luck (never on New Year's Day, which would sweep the new luck away), then share a reunion dinner — dumplings in the north, whole fish for abundance almost everywhere. Elders hand children red envelopes of lucky money, and hundreds of millions tune in to China's televised Spring Festival Gala, one of the most-watched broadcasts on the planet. Keep a lantern handy: the festivities close on day fifteen with the Lantern Festival, under the year's first full moon.

events.desc: Live countdown to the 2028 U.S. presidential election on November 7, 2028, how the date is set and how to register to vote.
events.intro: The next U.S. presidential election falls on Tuesday, November 7, 2028, the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November, as set by an 1845 federal law.

sections.p: Federal elections are held on “the first Tuesday after the first Monday in November.” In presidential years voters choose electors who formally elect the president and vice president through the Electoral College.
Registration deadlines and rules vary by state and close weeks before Election Day. Check your registration early at vote.gov so you're ready when the day arrives.

sections.h: Why a Tuesday in November? Blame the horse and buggy
sections.p: The 1845 law was written for a nation of farmers who might ride a day or two to reach their polling place. Sunday was for church and Wednesday was market day, so Tuesday won. November fell after the harvest but before hard winter, and "after the first Monday" kept voting off November 1 — All Saints' Day, and the day merchants settled their books. The first single-day national vote followed on November 7, 1848 — the very same calendar date as 2028.

sections.h: Getting ready long before the polls open
sections.p: You don't have to wait until 2028 to prepare. Checking your registration at vote.gov takes a few minutes, and in some states deadlines close about a month before Election Day. Most states offer early in-person voting or mail ballots, each with its own request window, and the rules differ if you've moved, changed your name, or vote as a student or from overseas. Your state or local election office website is the authoritative source for polling places, hours and ID requirements.

events.desc: Live countdown to the 2029 U.S. presidential inauguration on January 20 at noon, the constitutional date and its traditions.
events.intro: The next U.S. presidential inauguration is set by the Constitution for January 20, 2029, with the oath of office taken at noon Eastern on the steps of the U.S. Capitol.

sections.p: The 20th Amendment fixes the start of the presidential term at noon on January 20. The president-elect takes a 35-word oath, delivers an inaugural address, and a parade and balls follow.
Inauguration Day marks the peaceful transfer of power that has anchored American democracy since 1789. When January 20 falls on a Sunday, the public ceremony is typically held the next day.

Ronald Reagan's second inauguration, on January 21, 1985, is the coldest on record: 7°F at noon, after a morning low of 4 below zero. With wind chills near minus 20, doctors warned that marching bands would suffer frostbite within minutes, so the swearing-in moved indoors to the Capitol Rotunda and the outdoor parade was canceled outright — a scene that wouldn't repeat for 40 years, until bitter cold pushed the 2025 ceremony and parade indoors too. Thousands of student musicians who had traveled to Washington in 1985 played instead at a hastily arranged indoor event at the Capital Centre arena.

sections.h: How to be there at noon
sections.p: Tickets to the swearing-in are always free and are distributed through Congress: request them from your representative's or senators' offices, which take names in the weeks after the November election. No luck? The National Mall between 4th and 12th Streets is open to everyone without a ticket, with jumbotron screens and speakers carrying the ceremony. Every major network and C-SPAN broadcast it live, and the official schedule is posted by the Joint Congressional Committee on Inaugural Ceremonies.

Tied 21–21 at halftime, the Retrievers then poured in 53 second-half points on a Virginia defense that had allowed barely 53 per game all season, winning 74–54. events.desc: Live countdown to the August 2, 2027 total solar eclipse — the longest totality over land this century, crossing southern Spain, North Africa and Egypt. Path, timing and how to watch safely.
events.h1: Countdown to the 2027 Total Solar Eclipse
events.intro: On August 2, 2027, a total solar eclipse crosses southern Spain, Gibraltar, Morocco, Algeria, Tunisia, Libya, Egypt, Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia. Totality lasts up to 6 minutes 23 seconds near Luxor — the longest eclipse over land until 2114. This countdown runs to the event.

sections.p: The path of totality makes landfall in southern Spain near Cádiz and Málaga, crosses the Strait of Gibraltar into Morocco, then runs east across Algeria, Tunisia, Libya and Egypt — passing directly over Luxor — before continuing over Sudan, Saudi Arabia, Yemen and Somalia. A partial eclipse is visible across most of Europe, Africa and the Middle East.

Totality lasts up to 6 minutes 23 seconds near Luxor, Egypt. That is exceptional: most total eclipses give two or three minutes. This one is long because the Moon is near perigee (so its disc looks large) while the Earth is near aphelion (so the Sun looks small), and the path runs close to the equator, where the Moon's shadow sweeps across the ground most slowly. No eclipse over land beats it until 2114.
Never look at the Sun without certified eclipse glasses except during the brief moments of totality itself. A partial eclipse can damage your eyes even when most of the Sun is covered.

The previous total solar eclipse, on August 12, 2026, crossed Greenland, Iceland and northern Spain near sunset — the first totality visible from mainland Europe since 1999. Totality there lasted little over two minutes and came with the Sun low in the sky, which made for dramatic horizon views where the weather cooperated. The 2027 eclipse is the follow-up, and by almost every measure the better one: nearly three times the duration, a high midday Sun, and a path crossing some of the most reliably cloudless land on Earth.

events.h1: Countdown to the Perseid Meteor Shower
events.intro: The Perseids, one of the most popular meteor showers of the year, peak in mid-August, when Earth passes through debris left by comet Swift-Tuttle. This countdown runs to the peak night.

sections.p: At its peak the Perseids can produce 50–100 meteors an hour under dark skies, including bright fireballs. They appear to radiate from the constellation Perseus, hence the name.
No telescope needed, just get away from city lights, let your eyes adjust for about 20 minutes, and look up. The best viewing is usually after midnight.

Long before anyone knew what a meteor was, Europeans noticed shooting stars every year around August 10 — the feast of Saint Lawrence, martyred in 258 AD — and called them the 'tears of Saint Lawrence.' The scientific explanation arrived in 1862, when comet Swift-Tuttle was discovered, and in 1866 Italian astronomer Giovanni Schiaparelli matched its orbit to the August meteors. It was the first time any meteor shower was ever traced to its parent comet.

sections.h: 2027: a bright moon to work around
sections.p: The 2027 Perseids peak on the night of August 12–13 with the Moon about 80% lit — a waxing gibbous, and bright enough to wash out the fainter meteors for most of the night. The shower is still worth watching; you just have to time it. The gibbous Moon sets in the small hours, so the darkest and best stretch is the last hour or two before dawn, which is also when the radiant sits highest and rates are naturally at their peak. Keep the Moon behind you or out of view, give your eyes 20–30 minutes to adapt, and expect the brighter fireballs to punch through regardless.

events.h1: Countdown to the Geminid Meteor Shower
events.intro: The Geminids, often the strongest meteor shower of the year, peak in mid-December. Unusually, they come not from a comet but from an asteroid, 3200 Phaethon. This countdown runs to the peak night.

sections.p: Under dark skies the Geminids can deliver well over 100 meteors an hour, with bright, slow, often colorful streaks. They radiate from near the constellation Gemini.
December nights are cold but the show is worth it, no equipment needed. Find a dark spot, give your eyes time to adjust, and watch from late evening onward.

sections.h: The 121-year mystery of the missing parent
sections.p: The Geminids were first recorded in 1862, and for more than a century astronomers hunted in vain for the comet that produced them. The answer finally arrived in October 1983, when astronomers Simon Green and John Davies spotted a moving object in data from the IRAS satellite — the first asteroid ever discovered from a spacecraft. Within days, comet scientist Fred Whipple noticed its orbit matched the Geminid stream almost exactly. The parent wasn't a comet at all: it was asteroid 3200 Phaethon, named for the boy who drove the sun god's chariot, because it swings closer to the sun than any other named asteroid.

sections.h: A rare shower you don't have to stay up for
sections.p: Most meteor showers make you wait until after midnight, but Gemini climbs into the sky by mid-evening, so Geminids start appearing around 9 or 10 p.m. local time — one of the few major showers young kids can catch before bed. Rates keep building toward 2 a.m., when the radiant is highest. The meteors hit the atmosphere at about 78,000 mph — slow by meteor standards — producing bright, long, often yellow-tinted streaks. Bring a blanket, lie back, and give your eyes a full 30 minutes to adapt to the dark.

sections.h: The photo finish that took three days to call
sections.p: The very first Daytona 500, in 1959, ended with Lee Petty and Johnny Beauchamp crossing the line side by side at nearly 150 mph in front of 41,000 fans. NASCAR called Beauchamp the unofficial winner, and he celebrated in victory lane. Petty protested — "I had him by a good two feet" — and officials spent three days gathering news photographs and newsreel footage before reversing the call and declaring Petty the champion. The Great American Race was born with a controversy worthy of it.

sections.h: Watching from the grandstands or the couch
sections.p: On TV, the Daytona 500 airs on FOX, which locked up the race through 2031 under NASCAR's latest media deal. In person, tickets and infield camping are sold through Daytona International Speedway, and the race caps a week of on-track action — the Duel qualifying races the Thursday before set most of the 40-car starting grid, and grandstand seats for them cost far less than Sunday's. Commissioner Fay Vincent postponed play, and the Series didn't resume for ten days, still the longest pause in World Series history. When baseball returned, Oakland finished off a sweep — but the 'Earthquake Series' is remembered for everything except the score.

events.title: Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade {YEAR} Countdown: Date & Time
events.desc: Live countdown to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade {YEAR} on {DATE}. Steps off at 8:30 a.m. — time until the balloons fly down Broadway.
events.h1: Countdown to the Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade
events.intro: The Macy's Thanksgiving Day Parade {YEAR} is on {DATE}, Thanksgiving morning, stepping off at 8:30 a.m. This countdown ticks down to the giant balloons, marching bands and Santa's grand finale through the streets of Manhattan.

sections.p: Since 1924, Macy's has marched its Thanksgiving Day Parade through New York City, famous for its skyscraper-sized character balloons, floats and Broadway numbers. It airs nationally on NBC beginning at 8:30 a.m. in every U.S. time zone.
By tradition, Santa Claus closes the parade, unofficially kicking off the holiday season. The route runs through Manhattan and ends at Macy's flagship store in Herald Square.

sections.h: The year the balloons went to war
sections.p: In November 1942, with rubber and helium rationed for World War II, Macy's canceled the parade and donated its giant balloons to the war effort. At a public ceremony, Mayor Fiorello La Guardia accepted the deflated stars — about 650 pounds of rubber, destined for tires and life rafts — with the famous dragon balloon dramatically punctured for the cameras. The parade stayed dark through 1944 and returned in 1945, a joyful signal that peacetime Thanksgivings were back.

sections.h: See the giants inflate the night before
sections.p: The parade's best-kept open secret is the free balloon inflation event on Thanksgiving Eve, when crews spend about 90 minutes per balloon filling the giants on the streets around the American Museum of Natural History (West 77th to 81st Streets). On parade morning, claim a curb spot along Central Park West or Sixth Avenue by around 6 a.m. — skip Herald Square, which is reserved for the TV broadcast — or watch from home on NBC and Peacock.

facts: Held every Thanksgiving morning since 1924
Steps off at 8:30 a.m. local time
Famous for giant character balloons
Santa Claus traditionally closes the parade
About 3.5 million spectators line the route in person
Each giant balloon takes roughly 90 minutes to inflate with helium

timeline.text: The very first parade had no balloons at all — it featured a menagerie of live animals borrowed from the Central Park Zoo, including elephants, bears, camels, and monkeys.
Giant character balloons debuted, designed by puppeteer Tony Sarg and built with Goodyear, replacing the zoo animals after their roars scared young spectators.
Macy's began releasing the helium balloons into the sky at the end of the route as a finale, letting them float off over the city and eventually burst on their own.
The tradition of releasing balloons skyward ended after a loose Tom Cat balloon wrapped around the wing of a small plane over Queens, nearly bringing it down.
NBC aired the parade's first coast-to-coast national broadcast, turning the local spectacle into an annual TV tradition for families across the country.
The original Snoopy balloon, designed by Goodyear engineer William Ludwick, made its debut — the start of a run that would make Snoopy the most-featured character balloon in parade history.
Wind gusts over 40 mph battered the parade, and a Cat in the Hat balloon struck a lamppost and injured a spectator; the incident led Macy's to adopt new wind-safety rules for grounding balloons.

events.name: Rose Parade {YEAR}
events.title: Rose Parade {YEAR} Countdown: When Is It?
events.desc: Live countdown to the Rose Parade {YEAR} on {DATE} in Pasadena, the Tournament of Roses' flower-covered floats and bands. Time until the 8 a.m. PT step-off.
events.intro: The Rose Parade {YEAR} rolls down Colorado Boulevard in Pasadena, California on {DATE}, stepping off at 8 a.m. Pacific. This countdown ticks down to the Tournament of Roses' flower-covered floats, marching bands and equestrian units.

sections.p: First held in 1890, the Tournament of Roses Parade greets New Year's Day with floats decorated entirely in flowers and other natural materials, alongside marching bands and horses. It's followed by the Rose Bowl college football game.
By long-standing tradition, when January 1 falls on a Sunday the parade moves to Monday, January 2, so the date shifts by a day in those years.

The Tournament of Roses first added a football game in 1902 — and it went so badly that organizers dropped the sport for over a decade. Michigan demolished Stanford 49–0, and Stanford conceded with eight minutes still on the clock. Embarrassed officials replaced football with Roman-style chariot races down Colorado Boulevard. The gridiron didn't return until 1916, and that revived East–West matchup grew into the Rose Bowl Game, college football's oldest bowl.

sections.h: Curb camping or a grandstand seat
sections.p: Pasadena lets spectators stake out sidewalk spots from noon on December 31, and thousands camp overnight along Colorado Boulevard — folding chairs are fine, but tents, couches and ladders are banned. Prefer a guaranteed view? Grandstand seats are sold by Sharp Seating Company, the Tournament's official ticket partner. And don't rush off afterward: the floats park near Sierra Madre and Washington Boulevards for post-parade viewing in the days that follow, close enough to see every petal.

facts: Held in Pasadena, California since 1890
Steps off at 8 a.m. Pacific Time
Floats are covered entirely in flowers and natural materials
Followed by the Rose Bowl football game
The parade route runs 5.5 miles along Colorado Boulevard
The 'Never on a Sunday' rule dates to 1893, adopted so the parade wouldn't spook horses hitched outside churches

timeline.text: Pasadena's Valley Hunt Club, spearheaded by naturalist Charles Frederick Holder, staged the first Tournament of Roses on January 1, decorating carriages with flowers to show off the city's mild winters to friends back east.
The Tournament of Roses Association was formed to take over running the event, which had grown too large for the Valley Hunt Club to manage on its own.
A football game was added to help pay for the festival, becoming the first postseason college football game in the country and the forerunner of today's Rose Bowl Game.
NBC carried the Tournament of Roses football game coast-to-coast on radio, one of the first national network sports broadcasts in US history.
Actress Mary Pickford was named grand marshal, becoming the first woman — and first film star — to lead the parade.
NBC broadcast the parade nationally in color for the first time, making it one of the first coast-to-coast color telecasts in American television history.

events.name: White Day {YEAR}
events.title: White Day {YEAR} Countdown: When Is White Day? (March 14)
events.desc: Live countdown to White Day {YEAR} on March 14, Japan's answer to Valentine's Day, when chocolate gifts are returned. Time until White Day, to the second.
events.intro: White Day {YEAR} falls on March 14, exactly one month after Valentine's Day. In Japan and across much of East Asia, it's the day to return the favor: those who received chocolate on February 14 give a gift back. This countdown ticks down to it live.

sections.p: In Japan, Valentine's Day runs in reverse: women traditionally give chocolate to men. White Day, created by the Japanese confectionery industry in 1978, balances the exchange, on March 14, recipients return the gesture with white chocolate, cookies, jewelry or other gifts.

Tradition holds that a White Day gift should be worth roughly three times the Valentine's gift received, a rule of thumb known as sanbai gaeshi, the 'triple return.' The day is now celebrated in South Korea, Taiwan, China and beyond.

facts: Always on March 14, one month after Valentine's Day
Began in Japan in 1978
Returns the chocolate given on Valentine's Day
Also celebrated in South Korea, Taiwan and China

timeline.text: Fukuoka confectioner Ishimura Manseido, inspired by a reader's letter to a women's magazine lamenting the one-sidedness of Valentine's Day, created a marshmallow-and-chocolate sweet for men to give back to women and picked March 14 as the date.
Japan's National Confectionery Industry Association picked up the idea nationally, promoting March 14 as an 'answer day' to Valentine's Day and popularizing it as 'Marshmallow Day.'

The association rebranded the holiday as 'White Day' with the slogan 'Ai ni Kotaeru White Day' ('Answer Love on White Day'), widening accepted gifts beyond marshmallows to white chocolate and other sweets.
The reciprocal-gifting custom spreads to South Korea, where confectionery makers promoted March 14 alongside the country's own Valentine's Day chocolate-giving tradition.
The holiday spreads further across East Asia, with Taiwan and parts of China beginning to adopt March 14 gift-giving, each region adapting the custom to local norms.

The 'sanbai gaeshi' custom remains culturally familiar but is less strictly observed; the Japan Anniversary Association estimated the White Day market shrank from about 73 billion yen in 2014 to about 24 billion yen in 2021 amid what commentators call 'obligation fatigue.'

events.label: Juneteenth
events.name: Juneteenth
events.title: Juneteenth {YEAR} Countdown: How Many Days Until Juneteenth?
events.desc: Live countdown to Juneteenth (June 19), the history of America's second Independence Day and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: Juneteenth falls on June 19 every year, commemorating the day in 1865 when the last enslaved Americans in Galveston, Texas learned they were free. It became the newest federal holiday in 2021. This countdown automatically targets the next one.

sections.p: On June 19, 1865 — two and a half years after the Emancipation Proclamation — Union General Gordon Granger arrived in Galveston, Texas and issued General Order No. 3, announcing that all enslaved people were free. Celebrations began in Texas the following year and spread across the country.

After decades of state-level recognition and a national campaign energized in 2020, Juneteenth National Independence Day was signed into law on June 17, 2021 — the first new federal holiday since Martin Luther King Jr. Day in 1983. It's celebrated with cookouts, parades, music, red foods and drinks, and community readings of General Order No. 3.

facts: Observed every June 19
Commemorates General Order No. 3, read in Galveston, Texas on June 19, 1865
Also called Freedom Day, Jubilee Day and America's Second Independence Day
Became the 11th federal holiday on June 17, 2021 — the first new one since 1983

timeline.text: The first anniversary observances of General Order No. 3 were held in Texas, including a documented Houston gathering with a parade, church services, and a communal meal.

As millions of Black Texans and Louisianans joined the second wave of the Great Migration to cities like Los Angeles, Oakland, Seattle, and San Francisco, they carried Juneteenth traditions with them, planting the holiday outside the South for the first time.
Milwaukee held its first Juneteenth Day celebration, a modest block party that grew into one of the country's longest continuously running Juneteenth festivals.
A bill by Texas state representative Al Edwards made Juneteenth a paid state holiday, signed into law on June 7, 1979 and first observed in 1980 — making Texas the first state in the nation to do so.

At age 89, retired Fort Worth teacher Opal Lee set out on a symbolic 1,400-mile walk from Texas to Washington, D.C., part of a petition campaign for federal recognition that eventually gathered 1.5 million signatures.
South Dakota became the last state to establish Juneteenth as an official state holiday, completing recognition of the day across all 50 states.

records.label: Largest by attendance
records.value: The Philadelphia Juneteenth Parade & Festival, launched in 2016 with about 5,000 attendees, now draws more than 25,000 people annually

records.label: Longest-running claim
records.value: Two cities compete for the title: San Francisco's Fillmore District festival, founded in 1945, and Milwaukee's Juneteenth Day, held annually since 1971 and billed by the city as the nation's oldest

events.name: Columbus Day
events.title: Columbus Day {YEAR} Countdown: How Many Days to Go?
events.desc: Live countdown to Columbus Day (the second Monday of October), the history of the holiday and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: Columbus Day falls on the second Monday of October, marking Christopher Columbus's landing in the Americas on October 12, 1492. Many states and cities now also observe the day as Indigenous Peoples' Day. This countdown automatically targets the next one.

sections.p: The first recorded U.S. celebration was held in 1792, the 300th anniversary of the landing. Columbus Day became a federal holiday in 1937 and moved from October 12 to the second Monday of October under the Uniform Monday Holiday Act in 1971.

A growing number of states and cities observe Indigenous Peoples' Day on the same date, honoring the Native peoples who lived in the Americas long before 1492 — some celebrate one, some the other, and some both.

facts: Observed on the second Monday of October
Marks the October 12, 1492 landing in the Americas
A federal holiday since 1937; moved to Mondays in 1971
Observed as Indigenous Peoples' Day in many states and cities

timeline.text: The Columbian Order (Tammany Society) of New York held the first recorded Columbus Day celebration, marking the 300th anniversary of Columbus's landing with a procession, speeches, and a dinner.
Colorado became the first US state to make Columbus Day an official holiday, after Italian immigrant newspaper founder Angelo Noce lobbied the legislature.
President Franklin D. Roosevelt issued a proclamation designating Columbus Day a nationwide observance, following sustained lobbying by the Knights of Columbus and Italian-American advocacy groups.
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act, signed in 1968 and taking effect in 1971, fixed Columbus Day as a federal public holiday on the second Monday of October, moving it off its original October 12 date.
South Dakota renamed the holiday Native American(s') Day as part of a state 'Year of Reconciliation,' becoming the first state to officially replace Columbus Day on its calendar.
Berkeley, California, became the first US city to formally observe Indigenous Peoples' Day, holding the inaugural celebration on October 12, 1992, in place of the Columbus quincentennial.
President Joe Biden issued the first-ever presidential proclamation of Indigenous Peoples' Day, granting the observance federal-level recognition alongside Columbus Day.

events.name: Veterans Day
events.title: Veterans Day {YEAR} Countdown: How Many Days Until Veterans Day?
events.desc: Live countdown to Veterans Day (November 11), the history of the holiday honoring all U.S. veterans and a shareable countdown.
events.intro: Veterans Day falls on November 11 every year, honoring everyone who has served in the U.S. armed forces. The date marks the World War I armistice, signed at the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month of 1918. This countdown automatically targets the next one.

sections.p: November 11 was first proclaimed Armistice Day in 1919, a year after the guns of World War I fell silent. Congress renamed it Veterans Day in 1954 to honor veterans of every era. After a brief 1970s experiment moving it to a Monday, it returned to the fixed November 11 date in 1978.

Where Memorial Day remembers those who died in service, Veterans Day honors all who have served. Each year a national ceremony is held at Arlington National Cemetery's Tomb of the Unknown Soldier at 11 a.m.

facts: Observed every November 11
Marks the WWI armistice — the 11th hour of the 11th day of the 11th month, 1918
Renamed from Armistice Day to Veterans Day in 1954
Honors all who served, while Memorial Day honors those who died in service

timeline.text: President Woodrow Wilson proclaims the first Armistice Day on the first anniversary of the WWI armistice, calling for parades and a pause at 11 a.m. in gratitude for the victory.
Congress passes an act making November 11 a federal legal holiday, dedicated to the cause of world peace and celebrated as 'Armistice Day.'
WWII veteran Raymond Weeks organizes the first 'National Veterans Day' celebration in Birmingham, Alabama, campaigning to broaden the holiday beyond WWI to honor veterans of all wars.
President Dwight Eisenhower signs the bill amending the 1938 act, striking 'Armistice' and inserting 'Veterans,' officially making November 11 Veterans Day.
The Uniform Monday Holiday Act shifts Veterans Day to the fourth Monday in October, effective 1971.
The first Veterans Day under the new law falls on October 25 amid widespread confusion; most states reject the change and keep observing November 11 instead.
President Gerald Ford signs a law restoring Veterans Day permanently to November 11, responding to pressure from veterans' groups and state legislatures.

records.label: Largest Veterans Day parade
records.value: New York City's Veterans Day Parade, running since 1919, is widely cited as the nation's largest, drawing over 20,000 marchers and roughly 400,000 spectators along Fifth Avenue each year

records.label: Longest-running Veterans Day parade
