events.label: Clocks Fall Back
events.name: Daylight Saving Time Ends
events.title: When Do Clocks Fall Back? Countdown to Daylight Saving Time Ending
events.desc: Live countdown to when U.S. clocks fall back one hour — 2 a.m. local time on the first Sunday of November. Do you gain an hour? Yes.
events.intro: U.S. daylight saving time ends at 2 a.m. local time on the first Sunday of November, when clocks fall back one hour — the good one: you get an extra hour of sleep. This countdown automatically targets the next change.

sections.h: Which way do the clocks go?
sections.p: Fall back: at 2 a.m. the clock returns to 1 a.m., so the night is an hour longer. Phones and computers change themselves; ovens, cars and wall clocks are on you. Sunrise and sunset both arrive an hour earlier by the clock, which is why the evenings suddenly feel darker.

sections.h: Why the first Sunday of November?
sections.p: The Energy Policy Act of 2005 stretched daylight saving time to its current dates — second Sunday of March through the first Sunday of November — starting in 2007. Hawaii and most of Arizona sit the whole thing out and never change their clocks.

facts: Clocks fall back one hour at 2 a.m. local time, first Sunday of November
You GAIN an hour of sleep at this change
Hawaii and most of Arizona don't observe daylight saving time
The current dates have been in effect since 2007

timeline.text: The Uniform Time Act set the first nationwide fall-back date — 2 a.m. on the last Sunday in October — ending a patchwork of different local switch-over dates across states.
Congress amended the Act to move DST's start to the first Sunday in April, but left the fall end date untouched, so clocks kept falling back on the last Sunday of October for two more decades.
The Energy Policy Act of 2005 pushed the fall end date a week later, to the first Sunday in November; the new schedule was first used on November 4, 2007.

The US Senate passed the Sunshine Protection Act by unanimous consent to scrap the twice-yearly clock changes and make daylight saving time permanent, but the bill died without a House vote before that Congress ended.

The US House passed a revived Sunshine Protection Act 308-117 on July 14, 2026 and sent it to the Senate; if enacted, it would eliminate the fall clock change entirely by keeping clocks on daylight time year-round.

events.label: Clocks Spring Forward
events.name: Daylight Saving Time Begins
events.title: When Do Clocks Spring Forward? Countdown to Daylight Saving Time
events.desc: Live countdown to when U.S. clocks spring forward one hour — 2 a.m. local time on the second Sunday of March. Yes, you lose an hour.
events.intro: U.S. daylight saving time begins at 2 a.m. local time on the second Sunday of March, when clocks spring forward one hour — the rough one: the night is an hour shorter, and the evenings get an hour of extra light. This countdown automatically targets the next change.

sections.h: Which way do the clocks go?
sections.p: Spring forward: at 2 a.m. the clock jumps to 3 a.m., so you lose an hour of sleep — but sunset lands an hour later, kicking off the bright-evenings half of the year. Phones update themselves; the microwave does not.

sections.h: A century of arguing about it
sections.p: The U.S. first tried daylight saving in 1918, repealed it, brought it back in WWII as 'War Time,' and standardized it in 1966. Congress regularly debates making it permanent — the Senate even passed a bill in 2022 — but the twice-a-year ritual survives.

facts: Clocks spring forward one hour at 2 a.m. local time, second Sunday of March
You LOSE an hour of sleep at this change
First tried in the U.S. in 1918; standardized by the Uniform Time Act of 1966
Hawaii and most of Arizona never change their clocks

timeline.text: Germany and Austria-Hungary became the first nations to adopt daylight saving time, turning clocks forward on April 30, 1916 to conserve coal for the WWI war effort; Britain followed just three weeks later.
The US Congress passed the Standard Time Act on March 19, 1918, which both established the country's standard time zones and set the first federal daylight saving time, beginning March 31, 1918.
With the war over and the change deeply unpopular among early-rising farmers, Congress repealed federal daylight saving time in 1919, overriding President Wilson's veto.
President Franklin Roosevelt reinstated daylight saving time year-round as a wartime measure called 'War Time,' running continuously from February 9, 1942 to September 30, 1945.

The Uniform Time Act of 1966 standardized the national schedule, requiring states that observed daylight saving time to begin it on the last Sunday in April, while still letting states opt out entirely.

Responding to the 1973 oil crisis, Congress and President Nixon put the country on year-round daylight saving time starting January 6, 1974, but dark winter mornings and safety concerns collapsed public support, and President Ford repealed it that October after only about eight months.
The Energy Policy Act of 2005 extended daylight saving time by four weeks; the new schedule took effect in 2007, moving the start to the second Sunday in March, where it remains today.

events.label: Tax Day
events.name: Tax Day
events.title: Tax Day {YEAR} Countdown: How Many Days Until Taxes Are Due?
events.desc: Live countdown to Tax Day — the April 15 federal income-tax filing deadline — with the history of the date and what to do if you need more time.
events.intro: Federal income-tax returns are due April 15 (when the 15th lands on a weekend or a D.C. holiday, the deadline slides to the next business day). This countdown targets the next April 15 — file early and it's someone else's problem.

sections.p: The modern income tax arrived with the 16th Amendment in 1913, with a March 1 deadline. It moved to March 15 in 1918, then to April 15 in 1955 — officially to spread out the IRS's workload. It's been the most dreaded date on the calendar ever since.

Filing Form 4868 by Tax Day gets you an automatic extension to mid-October — but it's an extension to file, not to pay. Interest runs on unpaid balances from April 15 regardless. When the 15th falls on a weekend or Emancipation Day (a D.C. holiday), everyone gets a day or two of grace automatically.

facts: Federal returns are due April 15 (or the next business day)
The income tax dates to the 16th Amendment in 1913
The deadline moved from March 15 to April 15 in 1955
An extension moves filing to October — but payment is still due in April

timeline.text: The Revenue Act of 1861 created the first federal income tax to help fund the Civil War, temporary and repealed in 1872 — a rehearsal for the permanent tax that came 40 years later.

The 16th Amendment, ratified February 3, 1913, gave Congress the power to levy an income tax without apportioning it among the states, establishing the first permanent federal income tax with a March 1 filing deadline.
As the taxpaying population surged during World War I, Congress pushed the filing deadline back two weeks, from March 1 to March 15.
A sweeping rewrite of the tax code moved the deadline a full month later, from March 15 to April 15, effective with returns filed in 1955.
The IRS piloted electronic filing with just 5 preparers in 3 cities. Adoption snowballed — by the 2022 tax year roughly 97% of individual returns were filed electronically.
As an emergency exception rather than a rule change, the Treasury and IRS pushed the filing and payment deadline from April 15 to July 15, 2020, in response to the COVID-19 pandemic.

events.label: First Day of Fall
events.name: First Day of Fall
events.title: First Day of Fall {YEAR} Countdown: When Is the Autumn Equinox?
events.desc: Live countdown to the autumnal equinox — the first day of fall — when day and night are nearly equal everywhere on Earth.
events.h1: Countdown to the First Day of Fall
events.intro: Fall officially begins at the autumnal equinox in late September, the moment the sun crosses the celestial equator heading south. Day and night are nearly equal, and every day after is a little shorter until the winter solstice.

sections.p: Twice a year the sun sits directly above the equator, and Earth's tilt points neither hemisphere toward it. 'Equinox' is Latin for equal night — on this day nearly every place on the planet gets about 12 hours of daylight.
The full moon nearest the fall equinox is the Harvest Moon, which rises soon after sunset for several evenings in a row — the extra light traditionally let farmers keep bringing in crops after dark.

facts: Fall begins at the autumnal equinox, September 22–23
Day and night are nearly equal everywhere on Earth
The full moon nearest this equinox is the Harvest Moon
Each day now shortens until the winter solstice

timeline.text: The Maya built El Castillo at Chichén Itzá so that on the equinox sun, triangular shadows creep down the pyramid's staircase to meet a carved serpent head at the base.

China's Zhou Dynasty held a formal rite of 'worshipping the moon at the autumn equinox,' a court ritual that later evolved into the Mid-Autumn Festival, fixed by the Song Dynasty (960-1279) to the 15th day of the eighth lunar month.
Korea's Chuseok, still timed to the full moon nearest the equinox, traces to a month-long weaving contest held under Silla's third king roughly two millennia ago.

The Council of Nicaea anchored Easter's date to the vernal equinox, making the equinox central to the Christian calendar — a reckoning so far off by 1582 that Pope Gregory XIII overhauled the calendar to correct it.
The name 'Mabon' for the Wiccan autumn equinox sabbat was coined around 1970-74 by Aidan Kelly, who borrowed it from a figure in Welsh mythology to give the equinox a Pagan-sounding name.

Equinox does not quite mean equal day and night everywhere: the true equal-daylight date (equilux) falls a few days after the September equinox in the Northern Hemisphere, thanks to atmospheric refraction and the sun's disk width.

events.label: Winter Solstice
events.name: Winter Solstice
events.title: Winter Solstice {YEAR} Countdown: When Is the Shortest Day?
events.desc: Live countdown to the winter solstice — the shortest day of the year and the official first day of winter in the Northern Hemisphere.
events.intro: The winter solstice in late December is the shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere — and the moment the days start growing longer again. This countdown targets the next one.

sections.p: 'Solstice' comes from the Latin for 'sun stands still': the sun's daily path stops sinking lower and reverses. Ancient monuments from Stonehenge to Newgrange are aligned to this exact sunrise or sunset — people have been counting down to this day for 5,000 years.

The coldest weeks usually come in January — oceans and land keep releasing stored summer heat for weeks after the light bottoms out, a lag that also explains why the year's hottest days come after the June solstice.

facts: The shortest day and longest night of the year in the Northern Hemisphere
Winter officially begins at the solstice, December 21–22
Stonehenge and Newgrange are aligned to solstice sunlight
Days begin lengthening again immediately after

timeline.text: Ireland's Newgrange passage tomb was built more than a thousand years before Stonehenge and before the Great Pyramids of Giza, its stone roof-box engineered so a narrow beam of winter solstice sunrise lights the inner chamber for about 17 minutes.

Because only a handful of people can fit inside Newgrange's chamber, Ireland's heritage service grants solstice-morning access through an annual public lottery, drawing tens of thousands of entries for a few dozen spots.

Ancient Rome's Saturnalia was a week-long festival of feasting, gift-giving, and social role-reversal held in the days leading up to the solstice; its timing and customs later blended into the Christian Christmas season.

Across China, Korea, and Japan, the Dongzhi Festival honors the solstice with family reunions and symbolic foods — tangyuan rice balls in southern China, dumplings in the north, red-bean porridge in Korea.
Germanic and Norse peoples marked Yule near the solstice by burning a Yule log to coax back the sun and bringing evergreen boughs indoors for luck; both practices were later folded into Christmas.

events.message: The days get longer from here.

events.label: First Day of Spring
events.name: First Day of Spring
events.title: First Day of Spring {YEAR} Countdown: When Is the Spring Equinox?
events.desc: Live countdown to the vernal equinox — the first day of spring — when daylight overtakes the night for the bright half of the year.
events.h1: Countdown to the First Day of Spring
events.intro: Spring officially begins at the vernal equinox in late March, when the sun crosses the equator heading north and daylight starts outrunning the dark. This countdown targets the next one.

sections.p: At the March equinox the sun rises due east and sets due west everywhere on Earth, and day and night are nearly equal. From here to the June solstice, the Northern Hemisphere gains daylight at its fastest pace of the year.

The equinox quietly runs the Christian calendar: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the spring equinox — which is why it wanders across a five-week window from late March to late April.

facts: Spring begins at the vernal equinox, March 19–20
The sun rises due east and sets due west everywhere
Daylight grows fastest in the weeks after the equinox
Easter's date is calculated from this equinox

timeline.text: Maya builders at Chichen Itza aligned El Castillo so precisely that on the spring equinox the setting sun casts triangular shadows that appear to slither down the staircase to meet a carved serpent head at its base.
Nowruz, the Persian New Year, grew out of ancient Zoroastrian religious feasts; an 11th-century Iranian calendar reform later fixed it to the vernal equinox itself rather than a set calendar date.
The Council of Nicaea set the rule Christian churches still use: Easter falls on the first Sunday after the first full moon on or after the vernal equinox, which the council pinned to March 21.
Centuries of Julian-calendar drift had pushed the equinox back to around March 11; Pope Gregory XIII's calendar reform deleted ten days to restore it near March 21, the date fixed at Nicaea.
Angkor Wat's builders oriented the temple so that on equinox mornings the sun rises in line with its central tower, one of dozens of solar alignments identified across the Khmer temple complex.
A Life magazine story about Chinese eggs balanced during February's Lichun festival got reinterpreted by American readers as an equinox phenomenon; eggs balance the same way on any day of the year.

sections.p: Tadej Pogačar won again, and this one put him in the record books: a fifth Tour de France, level with Jacques Anquetil, Eddy Merckx, Bernard Hinault and Miguel Indurain, and nobody has ever won six. The Tour was created in 1903 as a circulation stunt by the sports paper L'Auto — whose pages were yellow, which is why the leader's jersey is too. The stunt outlived the newspaper by 80 years and counting.

Riders climb the equivalent of several Everests across the Alps and Pyrenees, burn 5,000–7,000 calories a day, and race for three weeks with two rest days. Roughly 10–12 million spectators line the roads — the largest live audience of any annual sporting event.

sections.h: Why 'Pomp and Circumstance' plays every single time
sections.p: Edward Elgar wrote the march in 1901 with no graduates in mind. When Yale gave Elgar an honorary doctorate in 1905, the band played it as recessional music — other schools copied the idea, and within a couple of decades it had become the sound of every American graduation. The tassel move is younger than it looks, too: turning it from right to left after the diploma is a mid-20th-century tradition that spread because it gives every graduate one perfect, photographable moment.

Roughly 3.5 to 4 million students graduate from U.S. high schools every year — the largest single class of graduates anywhere in the world. Ceremonies range from a dozen students in a gym to thousands in an NFL stadium, but nearly all share the same bones: a processional, a student speaker, the reading of every single name, and one glorious cap toss that most schools officially discourage and every class does anyway.

Every school's date is different — check your district calendar, then use the button below to create a countdown for your exact ceremony day and hour. Name it after your class ('Riverside High Class of 2027'), pick your school colors, and share the link in the group chat. Watching the same clock tick down together is half the fun of senior spring.

sections.h: From cherry orchard to comeback story
sections.p: Chico State opened in 1887 as the Northern Branch State Normal School, built on eight acres of cherry orchard donated by town founder John Bidwell. Its rowdier chapter is real: Playboy named it America's No. 1 party school in 1987, the same spring the 70-year-old Pioneer Days festival ended in riots and was canceled for good. The decades since have been a steady comeback — U.S. News has named Chico State a top public school in the West 21 times, and its agriculture, construction management, and AACSB-accredited business programs carry real weight across Northern California.

Commencement takes over University Stadium for a full late-May stretch: six ceremonies grouped by college, more than 3,700 graduates, and upwards of 26,000 friends and family in the stands. Around the main events, Chico State holds a constellation of smaller celebrations — the Nurses Pinning Ceremony, the Lavender Celebration, Latinx and Black graduation celebrations, and Project Rebound's ceremony for formerly incarcerated graduates. Expect North Valley sunshine and real heat; the morning start times are a mercy in Chico's May weather.

The Class of 1958 sent Don Young to Washington, where he became Dean of the House after 49 years representing Alaska; around the same time, a young Raymond Carver studied writing here under John Gardner from 1958 to 1960. The Class of 1975 gave tech Sandy Lerner, co-founder of Cisco Systems. Congressman Mike Thompson earned his bachelor's in 1982 and a master's in 1996, actress Amanda Detmer took her theatre arts degree in the early 1990s, and Chris Wondolowski left for the 2005 MLS draft and became the league's all-time leading scorer.

sections.h: From six graduates to a research giant
sections.p: Ohio State began in 1870 as the Ohio Agricultural and Mechanical College and graduated its first class — all six of them — in 1878. Today it is a research powerhouse with more than 61,000 students in Columbus, deep strength in engineering, business, and medicine, and a football culture with few rivals anywhere. The university's most famous 45 minutes may belong to Jesse Owens, the Buckeye sophomore who set three world records and tied a fourth in under an hour at the 1935 Big Ten championships.

Ohio State does commencement the hard way, and it's glorious: one ceremony per term with every college represented, and each graduate receives their actual diploma on the spot — a practice rarely attempted by a university this size. Spring commencement fills Ohio Stadium, the 102,780-seat 'Shoe,' on a Sunday at noon, and the surrounding weekend adds ROTC commissioning and candlelight ceremonies. Autumn graduates are not an afterthought either — December brings its own full commencement.

The Class of 1946 gave art its pop provocateur, Roy Lichtenstein, who stayed for a 1949 MFA. The Class of 1962 sent John Havlicek to the Boston Celtics, and 1965 handed R.L. Stine — editor of the Sundial humor magazine — to generations of goosebumped readers. Archie Griffin, football's only two-time Heisman winner, graduated a quarter early in 1976; Patricia Heaton took her theatre degree in 1980; Larry Sanger finished a philosophy PhD in 2000 and co-founded Wikipedia; and J.D. Vance, Class of 2009, rose to the vice presidency.

sections.p: The University of Alabama opened its doors in 1831 and has survived more than most campuses: Union cavalry burned it nearly to the ground on April 4, 1865, days before the Civil War ended, leaving only four buildings — among them the Gorgas House and the President's Mansion, which still stand today. The campus that once smoldered now holds a record 42,360 students as of fall 2025, drawn to everything from Culverhouse business programs to one of the country's best-known communication schools.

sections.h: A weekend of ceremonies at Coleman Coliseum
sections.p: Alabama graduates by college across a full weekend, and Coleman Coliseum's 14,619 seats fill several times over as the ceremonies rotate through. Tradition runs deep here: the Commencement 'A' symbol has marked the conferral of degrees since around the turn of the twentieth century, and the university confers degrees in May, August, and December, so winter graduates get a proper ceremony of their own. Cap-and-gown photos at Denny Chimes and Bryant-Denny Stadium are practically a required elective.

The Class of 1932 gave baseball its voice — Mel Allen, the Yankees' legendary announcer, who added an Alabama law degree in 1936. E.O. Wilson, Class of 1949, became the father of sociobiology; Gay Talese, Class of 1953, helped invent New Journalism; and Winston Groom, Class of 1965, wrote Forrest Gump. Sela Ward, Class of 1977, went from Crimson Tide cheerleader to Emmy winner, and Rece Davis, Class of 1988, hosts College GameDay. Joe Namath finally joined the Class of 2007, finishing his degree at age 64.

Ceremonies are grouped by college across the weekend, so confirm your graduate's exact day and time before anyone books flights. sections.h: From military college to Texas's largest campus

President James Earl Rudder, the Class of 1932 D-Day hero who led Rangers up the cliffs of Pointe du Hoc, opened admission to women in the 1960s and set the modern university in motion. Aggie graduation is a production: spring 2026 saw more than 13,000 diplomas awarded across ten ceremonies in four days, most of them in Reed Arena. The traditions land hardest here — many graduates finally turn their Aggie Ring so the class year faces outward, the way it's worn once the degree is earned, and the Association of Former Students welcomes every new graduate into the worldwide Aggie Network. December commencement is nearly as large, so winter Aggies get the full treatment too.

The Class of 1932 gave the world James Earl Rudder, who led Army Rangers up the Normandy cliffs and later remade his alma mater as its president. The Class of 1958's John David Crow won A&M's first Heisman Trophy in 1957 under Bear Bryant. sections.h: The oldest charter in American public higher education
sections.p: America's first state-chartered public university, Georgia has been teaching since before the U.S. Constitution was ratified. Today its Athens campus anchors one of the country's classic college towns, and its Grady College of Journalism administers the prestigious Peabody Awards. A defining chapter came in January 1961, when Charlayne Hunter-Gault and Hamilton Holmes enrolled as the university's first Black students; both graduated in 1963 and went on to distinguished careers in journalism and medicine.

Spring undergraduate Commencement happens on a Friday evening in Sanford Stadium, with graduates seated on the field between the famous privet hedges — the same "Between the Hedges" turf where the Bulldogs play. Graduate ceremonies are held separately the evening before. The most cherished ritual comes afterward: by tradition, students don't walk under the iron Arch on North Campus — its pillars stand for wisdom, justice, and moderation — until they hold a diploma, so graduation weekend brings long, happy photo lines beneath it. Many grads cap the celebration by ringing the Chapel Bell.

The Class of 1961 sent Fran Tarkenton from Sanford Stadium to a Hall of Fame NFL career; the Class of 1963 graduated Charlayne Hunter-Gault and Hamilton Holmes, who had desegregated the university two years earlier. The Class of 1982 gave ABC News its longtime correspondent Deborah Roberts; the Class of 1989 produced Natasha Trethewey, later a Pulitzer Prize winner and U.S. Poet Laureate. And Food Network's Alton Brown, who left Athens one credit short in 1985, finally collected his drama degree in 2004.

Sanford Stadium seats more than 93,000, so guest space is rarely the squeeze — Athens hotel rooms are. Book early for graduation weekend: rooms downtown and in Five Points sell out months ahead, and traffic builds fast before the Friday-evening ceremony. Arrive early to park and claim seats together, and watch the official commencement site for gate and bag-policy details. Counting down is better with company — share this page with your group chat, your family, and everyone flying in so the whole crew lands in Athens on time.

sections.h: From land grant to world stage
sections.p: Berkeley was born in 1868 as California's land-grant university and grew into one of the world's great public research institutions, famed for engineering, computer science, and the sciences; sixteen chemical elements were discovered here, including berkelium and californium, both named for the place. Its history is cultural, too — the Free Speech Movement erupted on the steps of Sproul Hall in 1964. A favorite detail: the mace carried at commencement is a bear-headed staff carved from wood reclaimed from South Hall, the university's oldest building.

sections.h: A river of blue and gold
sections.p: Commencement day at Cal is a river of blue and gold. Some 7,000 graduates and 23,000 guests fill California Memorial Stadium — a bowl that famously straddles the Hayward Fault — for the campus-wide ceremony, with keynote and student speakers and the chancellor conferring degrees. Graduates gather beforehand on Witter Rugby Field for photos and last regalia adjustments, then process into the stadium behind the university mace. Dozens of departments also hold their own smaller graduations in the same weeks, so many students get two ceremonies.

Class of 1912 alumnus Earl Warren returned for a law degree in 1914 and became Chief Justice of the United States; the Class of 1939 sent Gregory Peck toward Hollywood and an Oscar. Joan Didion, Class of 1956, defined a generation of American prose. Eric Schmidt finished his Berkeley PhD in 1982 before running Google; Steve Wozniak, having already co-founded Apple, came back to finish his degree in 1986. And the Class of 2010's Alex Morgan left Cal for World Cup glory.

Memorial Stadium is big, but Berkeley's graduation season is long — department ceremonies stretch across May, so confirm your specific dates before anyone books flights. East Bay hotels fill quickly for commencement weekend; look early in Berkeley, Emeryville, and Oakland, and lean on BART rather than hunting for parking near campus. Check the official commencement site for guest ticketing details as the date approaches. sections.p: Wisconsin's flagship was chartered in 1848 and built its reputation on the Wisconsin Idea — the principle that the university's work should benefit every corner of the state. Today it is a research powerhouse spanning everything from dairy science to stem-cell biology — human embryonic stem cells were first isolated here in 1998 — on a lakeshore campus where Bascom Hill meets Lake Mendota. Its most famous dropout may be John Muir, who studied here in the 1860s and said he left "the University of Wisconsin for the University of the Wilderness."

Spring commencement returned to Camp Randall Stadium in 2015 after a 25-year absence, and it now feels like a home football Saturday: Bucky Badger, the marching band, "Varsity" sung with arms swaying, and the whole class bouncing to House of Pain's "Jump Around" one last time. The bachelor's ceremony runs about 90 minutes at midday, while doctoral and master's candidates celebrate in a separate ceremony. Nearly 9,000 graduates crossed Camp Randall's field in spring 2026, with author James Patterson delivering the address.

The Class of 1929 included Eudora Welty, later a Pulitzer-winning storyteller; Gaylord Nelson finished his law degree in 1942 and went on to found Earth Day. sections.h: From 100 acres to the Cradle of Astronauts
sections.p: Purdue opened its doors in 1874 with six instructors and 39 students, five years after businessman John Purdue pledged $150,000 and 100 acres to found Indiana's land-grant college. Today it's a global heavyweight in engineering, computer science, agriculture and aviation — with undergraduate tuition famously frozen at 2012–13 levels. The nickname came from an 1891 jab in a rival's newspaper dismissing the football team as burly 'boilermakers'; students embraced the insult. Above all, Purdue is the Cradle of Astronauts: 30 graduates have been selected to fly in space.

Spring commencement fills the Elliott Hall of Music, a 6,005-seat proscenium theater slightly larger than Radio City Music Hall. Ceremonies stretch across a full weekend — nine of them honored more than 10,000 graduates in spring 2026 — and every single Boilermaker walks the stage as their name is read. Expect 'Hail Purdue' from the brass, a sea of gold tassels, and long photo lines at the Engineering Fountain and the Unfinished Block P afterward. A smaller winter commencement serves December graduates.

The Class of 1928 sent agronomy student Orville Redenbacher toward popcorn immortality, and the Class of 1932 graduated John Wooden, later basketball's most decorated coach. The Class of 1950 gave America astronaut Gus Grissom; the Class of 1955, Neil Armstrong, first person on the moon; and the Class of 1956, Gene Cernan, the last to leave it. Brian Lamb, Class of 1963, went on to found C-SPAN, and the Class of 2001 produced Super Bowl MVP quarterback Drew Brees.

sections.h: Planning your trip — and sharing the moment
sections.p: West Lafayette hotels sell out for graduation weekend months in advance, so book the moment your ceremony date firms up — or look across the Wabash to Lafayette. Spring ceremonies in Elliott Hall are ticketed, with each graduate receiving a set number of guest tickets, and doors open early for security screening, so plan a buffer. Each ceremony runs about two hours. If you're marching in 2027, share this countdown with your roommates, your lab group and your family group chat so everyone lands in town on time.

events.intro: Clemson University was founded in 1889 on Thomas Green Clemson's Fort Hill estate in the South Carolina Upstate, and graduation fills Littlejohn Coliseum each May and December. Spring 2027 ceremonies are expected May 5–7 per the university's proposed academic calendar, with the final schedule still to be confirmed. This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.h: From Fort Hill to a modern research university
sections.p: Thomas Green Clemson, son-in-law of John C. Calhoun, willed his Fort Hill plantation to South Carolina in 1888 to create a scientific and agricultural college; Clemson opened as a military school in 1893 and stayed one until 1955. Today it's known for engineering, business and the sciences, plus a dedicated automotive engineering research campus, CU-ICAR, in nearby Greenville. A defining moment came in 1963, when architect-to-be Harvey Gantt peacefully integrated the university — remembered as 'integration with dignity' — before graduating with honors in 1965.

sections.h: What commencement is like at Littlejohn
sections.p: May commencement spreads across three days at Littlejohn Coliseum, with roughly 5,000 Tigers graduating each spring in a series of college-by-college ceremonies. Clemson insists on the personal touch: every graduate crosses the stage as their name is announced. Many seniors already wear the Clemson ring — presented at its own dedicated ceremony each semester — and ROTC commissionings nod to the school's six decades as a military college. December brings a compact winter commencement, with nearly 2,000 more graduates crossing the same stage.

The Class of 1923 produced Strom Thurmond, later one of the longest-serving U.S. senators; the Class of 1938 gave Clemson its most beloved veteran, Ben Skardon, a Bataan Death March survivor who returned to teach English for two decades. Harvey Gantt, Class of 1965, became Charlotte's first Black mayor. Broadcaster Nancy O'Dell finished summa cum laude with the Class of 1990, future governor and UN ambassador Nikki Haley graduated in 1994, and quarterback Deshaun Watson completed his degree in just three years, finishing in December 2016.

sections.h: Planning your trip — and sharing the moment
sections.p: Clemson is a small college town, and graduation weekend swallows every hotel room in it — families routinely stay in Anderson, Seneca or Greenville, about 45 minutes away, so reserve early. Ceremony assignments by college are posted on the commencement site, and days differ by degree and program, so confirm exactly when your graduate walks before booking anything. If the Class of 2027 is yours, share this countdown with your classmates and your family group chat so the whole Clemson family counts down together.

events.intro: Auburn University has been the heart of Auburn, Alabama — 'the loveliest village on the plains' — since its 1856 charter. Spring commencement takes over Neville Arena at the start of May, with 2027 ceremonies on the university calendar for May 1–2, plus a fall commencement each December. This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.h: From East Alabama Male College to War Eagle
sections.p: Chartered in 1856 as East Alabama Male College, Auburn became one of the South's first land-grant institutions in 1872 and grew into a university known today for engineering, agriculture, architecture, pharmacy and veterinary medicine — its vet school, founded in 1892, is the oldest in the South. The 'War Eagle' battle cry has its own legend: at the 1892 Auburn–Georgia football game, a Civil War veteran's eagle supposedly soared over the field as Auburn drove to victory, and the crowd's cry stuck forever.

Auburn graduates cross the stage at Neville Arena, where spring commencement runs as a marathon weekend — eight ceremonies in spring 2026, when the university awarded a record 5,500-plus degrees to its largest class ever. Doors open 90 minutes early, names are read one by one, and scattered 'War Eagle!' shouts punctuate the applause. Afterward, families drift to Toomer's Corner for photos and fresh-squeezed lemonade from Toomer's Drugs, and more than a few graduates send a roll of toilet paper arcing into the famous oaks.

The Class of 1958 launched Ken Mattingly, who orbited the moon on Apollo 16; the Class of 1959 gave the engineering college its benefactor and namesake, Samuel Ginn. Astronaut Kathryn Thornton, Class of 1974, flew four shuttle missions; Tim Cook, Class of 1982, went from industrial engineering to CEO of Apple. Jimmy Wales, Class of 1986, co-founded Wikipedia; Octavia Spencer, Class of 1994, won an Academy Award; and Bo Jackson returned mid-career to finish his degree with the Class of 1995.

sections.h: Planning your trip — and sharing the moment
sections.p: Auburn-Opelika hotels command graduation-weekend minimums and sell out months ahead, so book as soon as your graduate's ceremony is posted — Columbus, Georgia, is a workable 40-minute backup. Check the commencement site for your ceremony's exact day and time, since colleges are spread across the weekend, and arrive early: doors open 90 minutes before each ceremony. Graduating in 2027? Share this countdown with your class group chat and let the whole Auburn family count it down with you.

events.intro: The University of Tennessee, Knoxville was chartered in 1794 as Blount College — two years before Tennessee became a state. Few schools send off their classes with a louder 'Rocky Top.' This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.p: Chartered in 1794 as Blount College, UT predates the state of Tennessee by two years. The 'Volunteers' name honors the Tennesseans who answered the call in the War of 1812 and the Mexican-American War, and the ethos survives in the Volunteer Creed's Torchbearer: 'one that beareth a torch shadoweth oneself to give light to others.' Today the flagship co-manages Oak Ridge National Laboratory with Battelle and is nationally known for supply chain management at the Haslam College of Business, nuclear engineering and its research ties across East Tennessee.

sections.h: Four days of ceremonies at Food City Center
sections.p: Ceremonies fill Food City Center — the 21,678-seat arena on the Tennessee River that Vol fans still call Thompson-Boling — spread across four days and split by college so every graduate's name can be read aloud. Graduate hooding gets its own ceremonies, orange is everywhere from stoles to socks, and no one leaves without at least one full-throated 'Rocky Top.' Afterward, the Torchbearer statue at Circle Park draws the longest photo line on campus. Winter graduates get their own commencement weekend each December.

The Class of 1910 sent Clarence Brown to Hollywood, where he directed Greta Garbo and earned the campus theatre that bears his name. Howard Baker, Class of 1949, became Senate majority leader and White House chief of staff; Jim Haslam, Class of 1952, captained the 1951 national champions and founded Pilot. Dave Ramsey, Class of 1982, built a personal-finance empire; Peyton Manning, Class of 1997, delivered Super Bowl wins in both Indianapolis and Denver; and Chamique Holdsclaw, Class of 1999, won three straight national titles with the Lady Vols.

sections.h: Planning your trip — and sharing the moment
sections.p: Knoxville absorbs 100,000-fan football weekends, so graduation won't overwhelm it — but downtown and Cumberland Avenue hotels near campus still book up fast, and four days of ceremonies mean you should confirm your graduate's exact date and time before reserving anything. Food City Center's size keeps guest seating comfortable, though parking lots fill early, so build in a buffer. If you're in the Class of 2027, share this countdown with your friends, your family and your group chat, and count down to Rocky Top together.

events.intro: Chartered in 1789, the University of North Carolina at Chapel Hill was the first public university in the United States to open its doors, and every May its Spring Commencement turns Kenan Memorial Stadium into a sea of Carolina blue. The university has announced Saturday, May 8, 2027 as the next Spring Commencement. This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.p: Carolina was the only public university in the United States to award degrees in the 18th century — its first graduating class, in 1798, was just seven students. Its very first student, Hinton James, famously arrived on foot in 1795 after walking from the Wilmington area. More than two centuries on, Chapel Hill is known for one of the nation's leading public health schools, the Kenan-Flagler business school, a storied journalism program, and a basketball tradition stitched into campus life.

Spring Commencement fills Kenan Memorial Stadium with thousands of graduates in Carolina-blue gowns — a truer shade introduced in 2011, when fashion designer and alumnus Alexander Julian ('69) redesigned the regalia in recycled-bottle polyester. Members of the 50th-reunion class march in to music from their own era, and in 2024 Carolina moved the ceremony to a Saturday under the lights for the first time, capping it with fireworks. The Class of 2026 alone numbered 7,183 new alumni.

The Class of 1818 sent James K. Polk toward the White House; the Class of 1920 gave American letters Thomas Wolfe. Andy Griffith earned his degree in 1949 before Mayberry made him famous, and Charles Kuralt, Class of 1955, went on the road for CBS. Michael Jordan left for the Bulls in 1984 but returned to finish his geography degree in 1986, a year before Stuart Scott, Class of 1987, headed toward SportsCenter. The Class of 1994 included soccer legend Mia Hamm.

Chapel Hill is a small town with a big graduation: hotels along Franklin Street and around campus sell out months ahead, and commencement traditionally lands on Mother's Day weekend, so families often stay in Durham or Raleigh and drive in. Kenan Stadium holds tens of thousands, but check the current guest and parking guidance on the official commencement site before you travel. Graduating this year? This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.h: From Deady Hall to TrackTown USA
sections.p: Oregon opened in 1876 with a single building and has grown into a research university best known for its journalism school, its sports-product ties, and track and field — Eugene calls itself TrackTown USA, and historic Hayward Field hosted the 2022 World Athletics Championships, the first ever held on U.S. soil. The school's most famous kitchen experiment came when coach Bill Bowerman poured rubber into his wife's waffle iron chasing a better running sole, a tinkering streak that helped birth Nike.

sections.h: A Monday morning in Autzen Stadium
sections.p: Because Oregon runs on quarters, commencement comes in mid-June, after most of the country has graduated. Starting in 2026 the university moved to a single university-wide ceremony in Autzen Stadium: graduates gather at the Moshofsky Center, enter through the west tunnel onto the field, and celebrate in a roughly 90-minute ceremony. Afterward, free shuttles loop guests back to campus for individual school ceremonies at Matthew Knight Arena, Hayward Field, and Beall Concert Hall.

The Class of 1934 gave Oregon Bill Bowerman, who returned to coach and co-found Nike with Phil Knight, BBA Class of 1959. The Class of 1957 produced novelist Ken Kesey; the Class of 1978, journalist Ann Curry; and the Class of 1986, Fight Club author Chuck Palahniuk. Actress Kaitlin Olson finished her theater degree in 1997, and basketball star Sabrina Ionescu earned her bachelor's in 2019 before addressing the university's 2020 graduates herself.

Eugene's hotels fill fast for graduation Monday and the weekend before it, so book early or look toward Springfield and the I-5 corridor. Autzen Stadium sits across the Willamette River from campus — many families park once and use the footbridge or the free shuttles rather than moving the car between ceremonies. events.intro: Founded in 1861 — twenty-eight years before Washington was even a state — the University of Washington holds one of the country's biggest graduation ceremonies each June in Husky Stadium, on the shore of Lake Washington. The 2026-27 academic calendar lists Saturday, June 12, 2027 for the Seattle campus. This countdown automatically targets the next ceremony.

sections.p: The University of Washington opened in 1861 as the Territorial University, on a downtown hill long since swallowed by the Seattle skyline. Today it is one of the West Coast's great public research universities, known especially for computer science at the Paul G. Allen School, UW Medicine, and public health. A nice touch of continuity: the four Ionic columns that frame the commencement stage are replicas of the columns that stood at the entrance of that original 1861 building.

sections.h: A stadium full of purple and gold
sections.p: Commencement day sends more than 7,400 graduates onto the field at Husky Stadium while roughly 50,000 family members cheer from the stands, with Lake Washington glittering beyond the east end. Each of the university's schools and colleges processes behind its own gonfalon — a Renaissance-style banner — and being named gonfaloniere, the student chosen by a dean to carry it, is one of UW's quieter graduation honors. Purple gowns and gold tassels complete the picture.

The Class of 1931 produced Nobel economist George Stigler; the Class of 1939 sent Beverly Cleary from the library school to Ramona Quimby. Bruce Lee studied drama here in the early 1960s and met his wife Linda on campus before leaving in 1964. The Class of 1975 included Linda Buck, later a Nobel laureate in medicine, while the Classes of 1986, 1995, and 1999 gave Hollywood Rainn Wilson, Joel McHale, and Anna Faris.

Mid-June is peak season in Seattle, so U-District and downtown hotels around graduation Saturday book up months ahead. The easiest arrival is by Link light rail — there is a station directly beside Husky Stadium — because Montlake parking and traffic get heavy fast. Watch the official commencement site in spring for the guest and ticket details for your year. Graduating Huskies: share this countdown with your class and count down to the stadium walk together.

sections.h: A land-grant school with a military heart
sections.p: Virginia Tech began in 1872 as the Virginia Agricultural and Mechanical College, and its Corps of Cadets has existed since that founding — it remains one of only six senior military colleges in the country, with about 1,400 cadets drilling alongside 37,000 civilian classmates. The university is best known today for engineering and technology, extending to a new Innovation Campus near Washington, D.C. Even the nickname is a piece of history: 'Hokie' comes from a made-up word in an 1896 student spirit yell.

sections.h: A Friday morning in Lane Stadium
sections.p: The university ceremony unfolds in 65,632-seat Lane Stadium under the motto Ut Prosim — 'That I May Serve.' One beloved quirk: the students who secretly performed as the HokieBird all year finally reveal themselves by wearing HokieBird feet in the procession. The Corps of Cadets holds its own graduation and joint commissioning ceremony, sending well over a hundred new officers into the Army, Navy, Marine Corps, and Air Force, while individual college ceremonies fill the surrounding days.

The Class of 1944 gave NASA its first flight director, Chris Kraft, whose name is on Houston's Mission Control. The Class of 1964 included Homer Hickam, the Rocket Boys memoirist, and the Class of 1969 a young Frank Beamer, who returned to build Hokie football. Kylene Barker, Class of 1978, became Miss America 1979; Regina Dugan, Class of 1984, became DARPA's first female director; Bruce Smith, Class of 1985, went first overall in the NFL draft; and Hoda Kotb, Class of 1986, woke America up on Today.

Blacksburg is a small town hosting one of Virginia's biggest weekends, so The Inn at Virginia Tech and nearby hotels sell out far in advance — many families stay in Christiansburg or even Roanoke, about 45 minutes away. Lane Stadium is roomy, but check the official commencement site for current guest, parking, and weather-plan details before you travel.
